video_title: AI Is Rewiring Retail Investing with Jim Swartwout & Jay Jacobs
gist: Two-part Risk Reversal episode: Guy Adami interviews Jim Swartwout (rendered as 'Jim Swartz' in the auto-transcript), CEO of Prosperum Fintech Holdings and a four-decade brokerage operator across Schwab, E*TRADE, Scottrade and Robinhood, on how AI bots, zero commissions and collapsed payment-for-order-flow economics are rewiring retail brokerage; then Dan Nathan interviews Jay Jacobs, BlackRock's US head of equity ETFs, on IQQQ, SOXX, tokenization, Korea's leveraged-ETF blowup and owning the full AI value chain. The connective thesis is access — fractional shares, low-share-price ETFs and private-market products keep widening the retail funnel while index concentration forces investors to take an explicit view on the Mag 7 and semis.

themes.theme: Retail brokerage economics after zero commissions

insights.claim: Payment for order flow has collapsed from roughly a nickel per share in the late 1980s to about $0.0001 per share today, which Jim Swartwout argues removes PFOF as a legitimate cost objection to retail trading.
insights.speaker: Jim Swartwout, CEO Prosperum Fintech Holdings
insights.so_what: With per-share order-flow economics this compressed, brokerage revenue growth must come from account growth, margin, lending and premium services rather than PFOF rebates.
insights.quote: payment for order flow was a nickel a share when I started. It's point zero zero zero one now. I mean, it's it's not a problem. It's never been a problem.

insights.claim: Swartwout says it is effectively impossible to compete on price in retail brokerage now that commissions are zero, so differentiation has moved to bespoke service, brokers with 20-plus years of experience and AI embedded throughout the platform.
insights.speaker: Jim Swartwout, CEO Prosperum Fintech Holdings
insights.so_what: Expect margin pressure and consolidation among undifferentiated fintech brokerage entrants; survivors monetize service layers, not trades.
insights.quote: it's hard to compete right now at zero commissions. You know, you have to differentiate yourself somehow.

insights.claim: Swartwout treats the move from 24/5 to full 24/7 equity trading as a certainty rather than a possibility, framing it purely as a question of timing.
insights.speaker: Jim Swartwout, CEO Prosperum Fintech Holdings
insights.so_what: 24/7 equities reshapes overnight market-making, clearing and staffing economics — an infrastructure build-out opportunity and a cost problem for brokers without overnight coverage.
insights.quote: You can trade 24/5 now at some firms. We're going to 24/7 without a doubt. It's just a matter of time.

insights.claim: Prosperum's Avant Garde broker-dealer launched its retail platform in April with equities, options and ETFs plus a partnership giving accredited investors access to private, pre-IPO names such as SpaceX, with futures and crypto still to come and crypto deliberately deprioritized.
insights.speaker: Jim Swartwout, CEO Prosperum Fintech Holdings
insights.so_what: Pre-IPO access is becoming a standard retail brokerage feature rather than a niche, while a brokerage CEO slow-walking crypto is a soft demand signal for retail crypto volumes.
insights.quote: Crypto's kind of in an odd place right now, so it hasn't been a rush.

insights.claim: Swartwout argues retail options are no longer treated as lottery tickets and that once properly educated, customers recognize options are not inherently riskier than other trades — with Avant Garde building a 10-part on-demand webinar series running from options basics to spreads and straddles.
insights.speaker: Jim Swartwout, CEO Prosperum Fintech Holdings
insights.so_what: Structural growth in retail options literacy supports continued expansion of retail options volume, a key revenue line for brokers and market makers.
insights.quote: once customers really understand stand options, they understand that they're not any riskier than most other trades.

themes.theme: AI bots as the new full-service broker

insights.claim: Prosperum's AI goal is to recreate 1980s full-service broker attentiveness — proactive account reviews, expiring-options alerts, roll suggestions — with no human on the line, with bots explicitly designed to be full-service brokers.
insights.speaker: Jim Swartwout, CEO Prosperum Fintech Holdings
insights.so_what: If AI collapses the cost of advice, the retail brokerage moat shifts from execution price to proactive account intelligence — a direct threat to human advisory and call-center cost structures.
insights.quote: We want our bots to be full-service brokers, basically. And we're on our way there.

insights.claim: Avant Garde already runs a customer-facing voice bot named Alex that discusses strategies overnight after 5:00 Eastern when human brokers are off-desk, alongside an internal bot answering account-level questions and a Winston AI partnership supplying research and analytics inside the trading app.
insights.speaker: Jim Swartwout, CEO Prosperum Fintech Holdings
insights.so_what: Overnight voice AI is the cheapest path to supporting 24/7 trading, and brokers buying rather than building research LLMs creates a B2B market for embedded financial-research AI.
insights.quote: We have a voice bot that can talk to you about any kind of strategy you want or anything else overnight when we don't have brokers there.

insights.claim: Prosperum offers letter-of-direction trading where a newsletter subscriber's recommended trades are executed automatically without the client placing them, and lets third-party trading communities route orders through its APIs.
insights.speaker: Jim Swartwout, CEO Prosperum Fintech Holdings
insights.so_what: Newsletter- and community-driven auto-execution converts social sentiment directly into mechanical order flow, amplifying the retail crowding effects discussed elsewhere in the episode.

insights.claim: Swartwout argues AI tools plus fractional trading have removed the capital barrier to portfolio construction, so a $500 account can now be managed like one that historically required around $10,000.
insights.speaker: Jim Swartwout, CEO Prosperum Fintech Holdings
insights.so_what: The addressable retail base expands downward in balance size, favoring platforms that monetize per-account rather than per-dollar.
insights.quote: you don't have to have, you know, $10,000 to trade. You can have $500 and still build a portfolio

themes.theme: Retail flow behaviour: rotation, community, and the death of day trading

insights.claim: From his six years at Robinhood, Swartwout observed retail flow always concentrating in one or two dominant stocks at a time, with the top name holding for months before flow rotated wholesale into the next one — a pattern he says is visible in daily market volumes and driven by social media discussion.
insights.speaker: Jim Swartwout, CEO Prosperum Fintech Holdings
insights.so_what: Retail crowding is serial and rotational, not diversified — a mental model for timing single-name gamma, squeeze setups and crowding unwinds.
insights.quote: retail tends to move in waves and they shift from one to another stock and you see one being the top stock for months and then suddenly the other one takes over.

insights.claim: Swartwout explicitly retires the 'dumb money' framing for retail, arguing that community debate before trades has left retail as well informed as professionals or better in some cases.
insights.speaker: Jim Swartwout, CEO Prosperum Fintech Holdings
insights.so_what: Strategies premised on fading retail as uninformed flow are increasingly mispriced; the remaining edge is in positioning and crowding, not information asymmetry.
insights.quote: we used to call, you know, pure retail dumb dumb money. I mean, it's not anymore. There's there's no doubt retail has as much information as anyone else, if not more in some cases.

insights.claim: Swartwout says retail behaviour has structurally shifted away from 1990s-style day trading toward weekly dollar-cost averaging into fractional shares and the thousands of available ETFs, which he argues mechanically props the market higher.
insights.speaker: Jim Swartwout, CEO Prosperum Fintech Holdings
insights.so_what: A persistent systematic retail bid explains dip-buying resilience and argues against expecting retail capitulation into drawdowns.
insights.quote: back in the '90s everyone was day trading. People aren't day trading anymore.

insights.claim: Swartwout names prediction markets as the single most surprising area of client demand and openly admits he does not understand why investors use them; he also notes client geographic interest has rotated from European markets last year back into US markets this year.
insights.speaker: Jim Swartwout, CEO Prosperum Fintech Holdings
insights.so_what: Prediction-market demand is running ahead of even veteran operators' expectations, while momentum-following geographic allocation means US underperformance would trigger an equally abrupt rotation out.
insights.quote: I think the one that surprised me the most is prediction markets. I don't quite understand why you would do prediction markets, but that's just my personal personal opinion.

themes.theme: Macro read: valuations, a sub-15 VIX, and the midterm setup

insights.claim: Swartwout names valuation as his single biggest market concern, drawing the analogy to the 2000 and 2007-2008 reversals and warning that when valuation resets happen they are brutal.
insights.speaker: Jim Swartwout, CEO Prosperum Fintech Holdings
insights.so_what: A brokerage CEO flagging valuation rather than liquidity as the risk supports positioning for a multiple-compression event rather than a flow-driven one.
insights.quote: valuation is the biggest concern I have with some of the companies that are out there right now.

insights.claim: Swartwout says this year's earnings have been exceptional with very few misses and small ones at that, but warns forward projected earnings must keep pace or current prices become a problem.
insights.speaker: Jim Swartwout, CEO Prosperum Fintech Holdings
insights.so_what: The bull case is explicitly earnings-dependent — forward estimate revisions, not rates, are the variable to watch for a top.
insights.quote: the forward projected earnings have got to keep up, or else we're going to have an issue with some of these prices.

insights.claim: With the VIX below 15 against historic single-stock volatility, Swartwout concedes the divergence is odd and inexplicable and reports heavy current client demand for portfolio hedges precisely because the setup is hard to explain.
insights.speaker: Jim Swartwout and Guy Adami
insights.so_what: Cheap index vol against expensive single-name vol is a live dispersion setup and makes index hedges cheap relative to realized idiosyncratic risk.
insights.quote: you have a VIX as we're sitting here today, which is south of 15, which to me is remarkable

insights.claim: Swartwout expects volatility to build into the midterm election as polls emerge, then predicts the market rallies after the election regardless of which side wins because the outcome itself removes uncertainty.
insights.speaker: Jim Swartwout, CEO Prosperum Fintech Holdings
insights.so_what: An outcome-agnostic post-election rally call makes the tradable variable the vol crush around the event rather than directional political positioning.
insights.quote: I think post-election, regardless of the results, the market's going to rally because it'll have more certainty, more clarity.

themes.theme: ETF proliferation and engineering around index concentration

insights.claim: An average of six ETFs launched every business day in the US in the first half of this year, and there are now more listed ETFs than single stocks in the United States — against BlackRock's roughly 1,700 ETFs globally.
insights.speaker: Jay Jacobs, US head of equity ETFs at BlackRock
insights.so_what: Product supply now exceeds underlying single-name supply, implying brutal fee competition and a coming shakeout of subscale funds.
insights.quote: In the first half of this year, there's been six ETFs on average launching every business day. And yes, there are more ETFs than single stocks listed in the United States now.

insights.claim: BlackRock launched IQQQ, an iShares Nasdaq 100 ETF, at 12 basis points waived to 10 through July 31, 2027, and deliberately set a low share price so an investor with as little as $25 can buy a whole share and options traders get a cheaper Nasdaq 100 underlying.
insights.speaker: Jay Jacobs, US head of equity ETFs at BlackRock
insights.so_what: A direct fee-and-share-price attack on one of the largest and most profitable ETFs in the market — watch QQQ's fee response and asset migration as the tell.
insights.quote: It is 12 basis points, way down to 10 basis points through July 31st, 2027.

insights.claim: With the top 10 Nasdaq 100 names — the Mag 7 plus three others — making up nearly 50% of the index weight, BlackRock split the index into QTOP (top 30 names) and QNEXT (next 70) so clients can express an explicit view on concentration rather than accept the index weighting.
insights.speaker: Jay Jacobs and Dan Nathan
insights.so_what: QTOP versus QNEXT is a clean pair-trade instrument for the mega-cap-versus-broadening debate without taking single-stock risk.
insights.quote: Like it or not, you really need to think about concentration as a function of the markets that we're in today, and it's really about bringing out more tools for investors to be able to express a view on it.

insights.claim: Nathan argues SOXX is better constructed than SMH because SMH's top two holdings, Nvidia and Taiwan Semiconductor, are a little more than 30% of that fund, while Jacobs confirms SOXX caps single-name exposure at around 7 to 8% across US-listed semiconductor companies and ADRs.
insights.speaker: Dan Nathan and Jay Jacobs
insights.so_what: Capped versus uncapped semi ETFs are materially different trades: SMH functions as a leveraged Nvidia/TSMC proxy while SOXX is the diversified sector expression.

insights.claim: Jacobs argues semiconductors have graduated in three years from an interesting cyclical subsector to a foundational component of the economy, such that every investor now needs an explicit view on their semi exposure the way they would for healthcare, financials or energy.
insights.speaker: Jay Jacobs, US head of equity ETFs at BlackRock
insights.so_what: Reframing semis as a core sector rather than a cyclical trade implies structurally higher baseline allocations and a lower cyclical discount for the group.
insights.quote: semiconductors went from kind of this interesting cyclical subsector to something that is now essentially a foundational component of our economy.

themes.theme: Tokenization, Korea's leveraged-ETF blowup, and the AI value chain

insights.claim: Jacobs frames tokenization as two payoffs — 24/7 global access to US assets and operational cost and friction reduction — but cautions the binding constraint is building a market-making and regulatory environment around it, not the technology.
insights.speaker: Jay Jacobs, US head of equity ETFs at BlackRock
insights.so_what: The world's largest asset manager treats tokenization as an access-and-cost story whose bottleneck is liquidity provision — favoring incumbent market makers over crypto-native rails.
insights.quote: if you expand assets to trade 24/7, that's one of the first considerations is building liquidity in a market making environment and a regular regulatory environment around it uh to promote market quality.

insights.claim: Korean retail investors have lost more than $35 billion in the recent KOSPI correction, with protests outside fund management companies, after SK Hynix and Samsung grew to a little more than 50% of the index and leveraged and inverse ETFs came to dominate KOSPI-related trading volume.
insights.speaker: Dan Nathan
insights.so_what: A live case study of concentrated index plus levered retail products unwinding — a template risk for US mega-cap concentration and the single-stock leveraged ETF complex.
insights.quote: since you had this correction over the last few weeks or so, you know, retail investors have lost more than 35 billion dollars.

insights.claim: BlackRock has deliberately never launched daily inverse or leveraged ETFs, offering delta-one country exposure such as its iShares MSCI South Korea ETF plus options-based income and buffer strategies instead, because levered products fail its three-part investment-rationale, client-need and product-quality filter; Nathan separately calls such products casino-like and says his shows have never advocated them.
insights.speaker: Jay Jacobs and Dan Nathan
insights.so_what: The largest issuer abstaining from the fastest-growing retail product category is a ceded revenue pool worth watching if regulators tighten — and a signal the flow lacks experienced-trader endorsement.
insights.quote: But today we have not brought out daily inverse or leveraged ETFs.

insights.claim: Jacobs sizes AI's economic impact at something on the order of $10-15 trillion over the next several years while stressing the theme is still early, and argues the hard problem is pricing something this early in its evolution.
insights.speaker: Jay Jacobs, US head of equity ETFs at BlackRock
insights.so_what: BlackRock's house number for the AI opportunity — the anchor behind its active AI product push and a benchmark for judging whether current AI valuations already discount it.
insights.quote: this could be, you know, something to the order of 10, 15 trillion dollars of economic impact over the next several years.

insights.claim: Jacobs argues the market has focused too narrowly on GPUs and hyperscalers and maps the fuller AI value chain as power infrastructure, physical data centers and their real estate, the wider semiconductor stack beyond GPUs including CPUs and memory, proprietary-data owners, frontier model developers, and AI-adopting application companies at the top — which is why BlackRock launched BAI, an actively managed AI ETF run by technology portfolio manager Tony Kim.
insights.speaker: Jay Jacobs, US head of equity ETFs at BlackRock
insights.so_what: A concrete checklist for diversifying an AI book out of the crowded GPU/hyperscaler trade into power, real estate, data owners and AI adopters — and BAI's holdings are a readable proxy for institutional AI value-chain positioning.
insights.quote: the markets have been really narrowly focused on just a couple of names and a couple of different components of the AI ecosystem.
